fields.question: Why measure sustained teaching activity rather than similarity in SGUID?
fields.answer: Relevant skills can teach poorly. Generate from verified traces and check early/late persistence and verifier agreement. Retrieval frequency isn't useful teaching count.
fields.example: A frequently retrieved but misleading skill shouldn't stay because it looks relevant.

fields.question: Why restore initial round weights after SGUID probing?
fields.answer: Probes already update the model. Restore to isolate training with compact selected library from extra probe learning. Next round generates new skills, not a fixed manual archive.
fields.example: Continuing after probing all candidates would retain discarded skills' effects.

fields.question: May SGUID delete negative coefficients, and how should negative results be handled?
fields.answer: No. The objective allows negative teaching signals. Check early/late activity and quality. Validation decline after two executed rounds remains a negative result, not success because the loop ran.
fields.example: Early gains don't justify retention if late signals fall below thresholds.

fields.question: Why restore round-start weights and retrain only selected skills?
fields.answer: Otherwise broad probe exposure confounds the compact curriculum effect. Reset, train selected skills, and regenerate from the updated model next round. Count sustained verifier-aligned teaching, not semantic matches.
fields.example: Testing ten hints gives extra practice; without a reset, later gain can't be assigned to the two selected hints.

fields.question: Why learn MetaOPD weights through a virtual student step?
fields.answer: Teacher gap does not reveal which signals improve tasks. Evaluate virtual updates against training-reference loss, use meta-gradients to learn weighting, then update the student with new weights.
fields.example: A large gap on a token may harm the reference task and deserve lower weight.

fields.question: How does differentiable virtual AdamW differ from scoring an actual step afterward?
fields.answer: Virtual step retains the graph to weight network for meta-gradients, while real update mutates state without that derivative. Optimizer state/order matter; arbitrary SGD isn't equivalent.
fields.example: Ask how weights caused the hypothetical change, not only whether a metric changed.

fields.question: What detaches in MetaOPD's 74-dimensional descriptors and weight transform?
fields.answer: Detach descriptors, not the weight network through the virtual step. Center per response, bound via tanh and normalize to mean one. Use new weights for real update; references come from allowed training data.
fields.example: Test references cannot supervise outer-loop weights.

fields.question: Why need a differentiable virtual update instead of weighting by current loss?
fields.answer: High loss can be noise. A virtual step reveals downstream reference-loss effects and meta-gradients, then real student update uses learned weights. Isolate descriptors, optimizer state and training-only references.
fields.example: Compare whether emphasizing a stylistic high-loss word or a reasoning token better serves the reference task.

fields.question: Why use synthetic scene coordinates as privileged Where-OPD input?
fields.answer: Generated scenes provide exact objects/positions for teacher while student sees image/question. Internalize spatial hints without coordinate access at deployment.
fields.example: Teacher knows positions; student learns left/right from pixels.

fields.question: How does spatial privileged text differ from ordinary text distillation?
fields.answer: The method needs matching actual scene images and spatial annotations. Random text distributions don't verify visual integration; privilege doesn't prove student reliance on images.
fields.example: A correct description paired with the wrong image still yields a computable loss but meaningless guidance.

fields.question: Does local Where-OPD generate scenes and load an MLLM?
fields.answer: No. It checks teacher KL under a spatial mask aligned to generated student positions, with frozen teacher. Random logits aren't visual evidence.
fields.example: Two hand-built left/right logits don't constitute image reasoning.

fields.question: Why give teacher textual coordinates while student receives only image and question?
fields.answer: Exact synthetic object/location metadata gives privileged scoring on student prefixes. Deployment lacks that metadata, so keep student inputs clean. Preserve spatial mask; random-logit tests don't prove spatial ability.
fields.example: Teacher can correct left-of-box relationships, but test students cannot be told coordinates.

fields.question: Why require every prefix to satisfy average cost in Weakest Link?
fields.answer: A final mean can hide bad early reasoning diluted by easy later tokens. First violation is absorbing. Costs are teacher negative logp.
fields.example: Appending common words cannot undo an unsupported prefix.

fields.question: How does absorbing penalty differ from a recoverable moving gate?
fields.answer: Violation persists even if later average improves. A rolling gate might reopen. This is a prefix constraint, not proof teacher cost equals task value.
fields.example: One high-probability next token doesn't clear the previous violation.

fields.question: May counterfactual current actions use different historical costs?
fields.answer: No. Start from actual prefix cost and vary only current action. Exact full-vocabulary immediate gradients coexist with sampled future returns. No full LM trainer.
fields.example: Inventing a worse history for an unfavored action invalidates its comparison.

fields.question: Why does an early violation persist instead of being diluted by easy later tokens?
fields.answer: Every prefix must meet teacher cost. Absorption blocks post hoc dilution; immediate counterfactuals vary only action at the real visited prefix. Teacher improbability still doesn't prove factual error.
fields.example: Adding common words after an unsupported derivation may lower final cost but cannot satisfy already violated prefixes.

fields.question: Why distill representations in PR-OPD rather than only final probabilities?
fields.answer: Hindsight skills create privileged hidden states. Align projected states at matching layers and response positions, then combine with task reward. Teacher skill is removed at inference.
fields.example: A retrospective tool principle can guide internal features without being deployment input.

fields.question: How do two forwards differ from concatenating skill to student context?
fields.answer: Run ordinary student and privileged detached teacher separately. Giving student skill changes deployment assumptions and can teach dependency. Representation matching isn't answer supervision.
fields.example: A tested student should rely on learned parameters when no skill text is supplied.

fields.question: What masks apply to layerwise PR-OPD alignment?
fields.answer: Align valid tokens of the same response at corresponding layers, excluding observations/padding. Skills come from completed training traces, not gold plans. Local kernel isn't agent training.
fields.example: Do not align extra teacher skill tokens to student response positions.

fields.question: Why forward the same response with/without hindsight skill rather than imitate skill text?
fields.answer: Compare how skill changes same-token/layer representations and transfer to an unprivileged student. Copying skill or teacher replies changes targets. Detach teacher, combine task reward and remove privilege at inference.
fields.example: A teacher can rescore an earlier decision using a validation reminder that the deployed student never sees.

fields.question: Why intervene only at MAESTRO's high-disagreement prefixes?
fields.answer: Teacher rollouts are expensive. Top-k coverage, similarity and early-position weighting allocate limited guidance. Disagreement doesn't automatically mean student error.
fields.example: An early fork can matter more than a punctuation discrepancy.

fields.question: Why combine coverage and Bhattacharyya similarity?
fields.answer: Coverage checks whether student candidates include teacher support. Similarity compares mass within shared support. Either alone misses differences; high PDS isn't teacher correctness.
fields.example: Identical candidates can have almost opposite weights.

fields.question: Does local MAESTRO generate takeover rollouts?
fields.answer: No. It computes top-k coverage, normalized similarity and PDS. Real intervention needs generation, state handoff and cost accounting; no measured call savings.
fields.example: Hand-entered probabilities can trigger a score without any teacher rollout.

fields.question: Why use both top-k coverage and Bhattacharyya similarity for interventions?
fields.answer: One checks support inclusion, the other shared probability allocation. Disagreement and position weight prioritize scarce teacher compute. It is a clue, not correctness; local PDS doesn't generate a takeover.
fields.example: Two models can share identical top-k words while assigning very different probabilities.
